questions.q: State the complement rule for probability.
questions.a: P(not E) = 1 − P(E), where "not E" is the complement of event E. A wrong answer (e.g., "P(not E) = P(E)") shows the student does not understand the relationship between an event and its complement.
P(not E) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7. A wrong answer (e.g., 0.3 or −0.3) shows the student cannot apply the complement formula.

questions.q: A die is rolled. What is the probability of NOT getting a prime number?
questions.a: P(prime) = 3/6 = 1/2 (primes: 2, 3, 5). P(not prime) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2. (Non-primes: 1, 4, 6 — note 1 is not prime.) A wrong answer (e.g., 3/6 = 1/2 without showing the complement step, or including 1 as prime) shows incomplete reasoning or a number theory error.

The sample space S is the union of E and "not E", and they are mutually exclusive (an outcome either is in E or is not, but not both). So P(E) + P(not E) = P(S) = 1. A wrong answer (e.g., "because they are the same event") shows the student does not understand that E and not E partition the sample space.

questions.q: A bag has 10 balls, 4 of which are defective. What is the probability of drawing a non-defective ball?
questions.a: P(defective) = 4/10 = 2/5. P(non-defective) = 1 − 2/5 = 3/5. (Directly: 6 non-defective out of 10, P = 6/10 = 3/5.) A wrong answer (e.g., 4/10) shows the student computed P(defective) instead of P(non-defective).

questions.q: Three coins are tossed. Use the complement rule to find the probability of getting at least one head.
questions.a: P(at least one head) = 1 − P(no heads) = 1 − P(TTT) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. The complement of "at least one head" is "no heads" (all tails), which is easier to compute. A wrong answer (e.g., listing all 7 favourable outcomes and getting 7/8 without using the complement) is correct but misses the efficiency of the method.
